newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia swings to huge trade deficit in Jun.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia swings to huge trade deficit in Jun.

text.p: Big purchases of ships and planes propelled Malaysia's trade balance to deficit of 2.8 billion ringgit ($1.08 billion) in June against a surplus of 156.2 million in May, the Statistics Department said on Monday.
Exports in June totalled 16.5 billion ringgit against imports of 19.3 billion, the department said.
"On the surface, it's quite a huge figure and above market expectations. It was very much inflated by imports of bulky items again," said Kevin Chew, chief economist at Caspian Securities.

The department said June's deficit was caused by the purchase of ships and tankers, including a liquefied natural gas carrier, and commercial aircraft, amounting to 2.2 billion ringgit or 11.4 percent of total imports.

"The key thing to watch is whether exports will improve in the second half of the year," Chew said. "Those who were expecting an improvement in the current account deficit this year will probably have to revise their numbers."
In the first six months of this year, Malaysia posted a deficit of 2.7 billion ringgit against a deficit of 687.8 million in the same period last year.
Imports in the six month period were at 101.1 billion ringgit, up 3.9 billion ringgit or four percent, compared with the 97.2 billion registered in the same period last year.
Exports, on the other hand, rose by only 1.8 billion ringgit or 1.9 percent, to 98.4 billion from 96.6 billion in the first six months of 1996.

"One encouraging thing is that exports are up year on year," said P.K. Basu, regional economist at UBS Securities in Singapore. Semiconductors declined year-on-year for the first six months, but the big swing factor has been transportation equipment. The sheer size of June's equipment imports boggles the mind."
"Lumpy" or big-ticket import items, such as transport equipment, totalled 4.9 billion ringgit in the first half of this year alone against 3.8 billion in 1996, the Statistics Department said.
Kostas Panagiotou, senior economist at Kim Eng Securities, said "the figure was shocking".

"It doesn't look encouraging at all. The fact that exports are still not picking up is very worrying," Panagiotou said. "The stock market was already talking about a large deficit today. Confirmation of it will trigger further downside in the market tomorrow."

The key Composite Index on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange -- which has been in a four-month slump anyway -- closed down 24.07 points, or 2.40 percent, to 978.56 on Monday, partly on worries about the trade figure.

Part of the reason for weak export growth in the first half of 1997 was declining export earnings in some of Malaysia's key commodities, including rubber, crude oil and sawn timber, the Statistics Department said.
